title: 3-Read Friday #72: AI Assessment, Questioning, and Participation
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #72 pairs a high-stakes policy piece with two classroom-level pieces on getting students to participate well. Daisy Christodoulou argues that generative AI has already broken England's written-assessment system and lays out five concrete recommendations for the government's curriculum and assessment review, from reviewing AI marking systems to keeping handwritten exams. Christian Moore Anderson diagnoses why open classroom questions so often fail - students face an unbounded, ambiguous set of possible answers and effectively freeze - and proposes reformulating questions around differences to sharply narrow and clarify what's being asked. Mason Davies extends a related idea from Adam Boxer's 'front-loading the means of participation,' showing concrete examples of how making participation expectations explicit and early eliminates wasted lesson time. Barton's own commentary threads a shared concern through all three: much of what goes wrong in classrooms and in assessment policy traces back to ambiguity about what, exactly, students are being asked to do.
points: Daisy Christodoulou's headline argument: AI use among UK secondary students jumped from 37% to 77% between 2023 and 2024, and AI detectors 'don't work' - the growing, undetectable use of generative AI now threatens the integrity of written assessment itself.

Christodoulou's five recommendations for England's curriculum and assessment review: review AI marking systems, revise initial teacher training on assessment and AI, eliminate non-examined written coursework, keep handwritten exams, and investigate post-qualification university admissions.

Christian Moore Anderson's diagnosis of failed questioning: open, single-concept questions leave students facing an unbounded field of possible answers, causing a kind of mental paralysis that reads to teachers as random or disengaged responses.

Moore Anderson's fix - asking questions about differences rather than single concepts - establishes 'common ground' so students know exactly what aspect they're being asked to compare, sharply increasing participation.

Mason Davies's related classroom technique, 'front-loading the means of participation' (from Adam Boxer), places the instruction for how students should respond before the content itself, so students aren't still processing 'how do I answer?' after they've missed the question.
quotes: Absolute gold from Daisy, the Queen of Assessment. With my maths teacher hat on, I have to ask what the future of maths homework is when students can bang pretty much any question into ChatGPT (or equivalent) and get the correct answer?
Christian shows how a simple reformulation of a question - namely, focusing on differences - can focus students' attention on a key aspect, boosting participation.
This is presented in the context of teaching biology, but can be applied to any subject.
On one of Adam Boxer's appearances on my podcast, he shared a strategy called front-loading the means of participation.
This simple tweak to the order in which we present instructions to students is a game-changer in reducing wasted time in lessons.
